member.name: T:SupplyChain.Domain.Common.ICompanyScoped
member.summary: Marks an entity that belongs to exactly one company (tenant).

remarks.para: The legacy system achieved tenancy by keeping 18 separate SQL Server databases with an identical schema — InventoryPJL, InventoryUJL, InventoryPAL and so on — and switching the connection string at login. Master data was replicated into all of them by executing the same INSERT up to seventeen times in sequence, untransacted.

The modern design consolidates those into one database and scopes transactional data by . Every entity implementing this interface receives an EF Core global query filter, so tenant isolation is enforced in the data layer and cannot be bypassed by forgetting a WHERE clause. Master data (suppliers, items, parties) is deliberately not company-scoped: it was always logically global.

member.name: T:SupplyChain.Domain.ValueObjects.DocumentNumber
member.summary: A user-facing business document number, scoped to a company and a year.

remarks.para: The legacy numbering tables (NEW_PI, New_MRR, New_SCID, New_ACCID) each stored the same triple: a sequence number (PI_No), a year (PI_Year) and a pre-formatted display string (PINo). Storing the formatted string alongside its own components meant the two could — and over eighteen databases almost certainly did — drift apart.
Here the components are stored and the display form is derived, so they cannot disagree.

This is deliberately distinct from . The legacy application used one MAX(id) + 1 value for both the primary key and the printed document number, which conflated a storage concern with a business identifier that appears on paperwork and is quoted by suppliers. Splitting them lets the surrogate key be a plain IDENTITY while the document number keeps its gap-free, per-company, per-year sequence.
